note: Explains proxy discrimination persisting after sensitive attributes are removed, which is the point clients most often get wrong.
title: Algorithmic Bias: From Discrimination Discovery to Fairness-aware Data Mining
journal: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
explain_beginner: This paper looks at whether computer programs that make decisions about people can treat some groups unfairly. The answer is yes. For example, studies found that job ads for well paid work were shown to men more often than women, and ads about arrest records appeared more often with searches for black names. This can happen even when the people who built the program did not mean to be unfair. It can come from the data itself, which may carry the effects of past unfair treatment. The authors say we need to build these systems with fairness in mind from the start.
explain_business: This paper matters for any organization using data driven decisions in areas like hiring, lending, housing, or advertising. It shows that unfair outcomes can occur even when sensitive fields such as gender or ethnicity are removed from the data, because other variables can act as proxies through correlations. Removing the obvious attribute is therefore not enough to prevent discrimination. The practical implication is that fairness needs to be designed into these systems from the start, and that leaders should treat bias as a real risk in analytics projects rather than assuming good intentions are sufficient.
explain_practitioner: The authors survey algorithmic discrimination in data driven decision making across domains such as finance, health, hiring, housing, and education. They note that bias can arise without discriminatory intent, either because the underlying data reflects or amplifies historical discrimination, or because a trained model can still discriminate on sensitive attributes even after those attributes are removed from the input, due to correlations present in the data. They cite online advertising studies as evidence. The paper argues for data mining systems that are discrimination conscious by design and frames this as a new, challenging research area.
